Split the initial activity between the two substances, then decay each separately.
**Step 1 — relate the two initial activities.** With equal numbers of atoms N₀ and
λ = 0·693/T:
λ_A = 0·693/1 and λ_B = 0·693/2, so **λ_A = 2λ_B** ✓
Activity is λN₀, so
**A's activity is twice B's** at the start ✓
**Step 2 — divide the 1200.** In the ratio 2 : 1,
A₀(A) = **800** dis/min
A₀(B) = **400** dis/min ✓
**Step 3 — decay each over 4 days.**
**A**, half-life 1 day: **4** half-lives, so 800/2⁴ = 800/16 = **50** dis/min ✓
**B**, half-life 2 days: **2** half-lives, so 400/2² = 400/4 = **100** dis/min ✓
**Step 4 — add.**
50 + 100 = **150 dis/min** ✓
**Why B ends up the more active.** A starts twice as strong but burns out **four times**
faster ✓ By day 4 the positions have reversed, and B contributes two thirds of what
remains.
**When the two are equally active.** Setting 800(½)^t = 400(½)^(t/2) gives
(½)^(t/2) = ½, so **t = 2 days** ✓ Before then A dominates; after, B does.
**Why equal numbers of atoms do not mean equal activities.** Activity is **λN**, and the
shorter-lived nuclide has the larger λ ✓ A nuclide with a half-life of seconds is
furiously active; one with a half-life of millions of years is barely detectable, for
the same number of atoms.
**A table of the decline.**
day 0: 800 + 400 = **1200**
day 1: 400 + 283 = **683**
day 2: 200 + 200 = **400**
day 3: 100 + 141 = **241**
day 4: 50 + 100 = **150** ✓
**Why the total is not a simple exponential.** A sum of two exponentials with different
constants is **not** itself an exponential ✓ The combined curve steepens early, while
the short-lived component dominates, then flattens as only the long-lived one remains -
which is exactly why such mixtures must be treated component by component.
**Reading the distractors.** **200**, **250** and **500 dis/min** ✗ would follow from
splitting the 1200 equally, or from applying one half-life to both ✓
∴ 150 dis/min.

**Energy** is a scalar; the other three carry a direction.
**Step 1 — classify each quantity.**
**weight** - the gravitational force on a body, always directed **downward**:
**vector** ✓
**nuclear spin** - an intrinsic **angular momentum**, with a direction along the spin
axis: **vector** ✓
**momentum** - mv, pointing along the velocity: **vector** ✓
**potential energy** - a single number of joules, with no direction at all:
**scalar** ✓
**Step 2 — conclude.** **Potential energy** is the odd one out ✓
**Why energy cannot have a direction.** It is defined through a **dot product**,
W = F̄·d̄s̄ ✓ A dot product of two vectors is always a scalar - which is why work,
kinetic energy and potential energy are all scalars, even though force and displacement
are vectors.
**Why energy may be negative without being a vector.** Gravitational potential energy is
negative below the reference level, and electrostatic potential energy is negative for
opposite charges ✓ A **sign** is not a direction: it says "less than the reference", not
"pointing backwards".
**Why weight is a vector but mass is not.** Mass is a scalar amount of matter; weight is
the **force** mg, with a direction ✓ The two are often confused in everyday speech but
are different kinds of quantity.
**Why nuclear spin is a vector.** It is angular momentum, quantised in units of ℏ and
oriented along an axis ✓ Its direction is physically real: it determines how a nucleus
responds to a magnetic field, which is the whole basis of **NMR** and **MRI**.
**The test to apply.** Does the quantity obey the **triangle law of addition**, and
does it change when the axes are rotated? ✓ Momentum and weight do; potential energy
does not - every observer, however oriented, assigns it the same number.
**Other common scalars.** Mass, time, charge, temperature, speed, distance, work,
power, density, pressure ✓
**Other common vectors.** Displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, torque, impulse,
electric and magnetic field, angular momentum ✓
∴ Potential energy.

For hydrogen, E_n = **−13·6/n²** eV, so the third orbit is at −13·6/9.
**Step 1 — write the energy formula.**
E_n = **−13·6/n² eV** ✓
**Step 2 — substitute n = 3.**
E₃ = −13·6/9
= **−1·51 eV** ✓
and the magnitude asked for is **1·51 eV** ✓
**Why the energy is negative.** The zero is taken at **infinite separation** with the
electron at rest ✓ A bound electron has less energy than that, so its energy is
negative. The magnitude 1·51 eV is the energy needed to **remove** it from the third
orbit - the ionisation energy from that level.
**The first few levels.**
n = 1: **−13·60 eV** - the ground state
n = 2: **−3·40 eV**
n = 3: **−1·51 eV** ✓
n = 4: **−0·85 eV**
n = ∞: **0**
**Why the levels crowd together.** The 1/n² dependence means the spacing shrinks
rapidly ✓ The gap from n = 1 to 2 is 10·2 eV; from 3 to 4 only 0·66 eV. That crowding
is why spectral series converge to a limit.
**Where this level shows itself.** Transitions **down** to n = 3 give the **Paschen**
series, in the infrared; transitions **from** n = 3 to n = 2 give the red **H_α** line
at 656 nm ✓
**The other quantities at n = 3.**
radius: r = 9 x 0·529 = **4·76 Å** ✓
speed: v = (2·18 x 10⁶)/3 = **7·3 x 10⁵ m s⁻¹**
The electron is nine times further out and three times slower than in the ground state.
**The virial relation.** Kinetic energy = **+1·51 eV**, potential energy = **−3·02 eV**,
total **−1·51 eV** ✓ The total is always equal in magnitude to the kinetic energy and
half the potential - a general property of inverse-square binding.
**Reading the distractors.** **3·4 eV** ✗ is the n = 2 level. **4·53 eV** ✗ is 13·6/3,
dividing by n rather than n², and **4 eV** ✗ is a rounding of that ✓ The square is the
step that matters.
∴ 1.51 eV.

A force that is the **same** between proton-proton and proton-neutron pairs must be
**charge-independent** - the hallmark of the **strong nuclear force**.
**Step 1 — test the electrical force.** A **neutron is uncharged**, so the
electrostatic force between a proton and a neutron is **zero** ✗ It cannot possibly
equal the proton-proton repulsion. The electrical force is ruled out at once.
**Step 2 — test gravity.** It depends on **mass**, and the proton and neutron have very
nearly equal masses - so it is indeed almost the same for both pairs ✓ But gravity
between nucleons is about **10⁻³⁸** of the strong force ✗ far too feeble to bind
anything, let alone hold a nucleus together.
**Step 3 — test the weak force.** It acts only in processes that **change** particle
identity, such as beta decay ✗ It is not a binding force and does not hold nucleons
together.
**Step 4 — identify the strong force.** It is **charge-independent**: the n-p, p-p and
n-n interactions are essentially identical ✓ This is one of its defining properties,
and exactly what the question describes.
**Why charge independence matters.** It means the strong force sees a proton and a
neutron as two states of one particle, the **nucleon** ✓ Heisenberg captured this with
the idea of **isospin**, a formal symmetry that has guided nuclear and particle physics
ever since.
**The evidence for it.** **Mirror nuclei** - pairs such as ³H and ³He, with the numbers
of protons and neutrons exchanged - have nearly identical binding energies ✓ The small
difference is entirely accounted for by the extra **Coulomb** repulsion in ³He.
**The strong force's other properties.**
**short range**, about 10⁻¹⁵ m, falling away exponentially beyond ✓
**attractive** at normal nucleon spacing but strongly **repulsive** below about 0·5 fm,
which is what stops a nucleus collapsing ✓
**saturating** - each nucleon binds only to its neighbours, which is why binding energy
per nucleon is roughly constant.
**The relative strengths.** strong **1**, electromagnetic **10⁻²**, weak **10⁻¹³**,
gravitational **10⁻³⁸** ✓
∴ Strong nuclear force.

Equal and opposite momenta, with masses set by the **cubes** of the radii.
**Step 1 — relate the masses to the radii.** Nuclear matter has constant density, so
m ∝ R³ ✓
With radii in the ratio 1 : 2,
**m₁ : m₂ = 1 : 8** ✓
**Step 2 — conserve momentum.** The parent is at rest, so
m₁v₁ = m₂v₂ ✓
**Step 3 — form the velocity ratio.**
v₁/v₂ = m₂/m₁
= **8 : 1** ✓
**Why the velocities go inversely as the masses.** Equal momenta shared between unequal
masses means the light fragment must move faster, in exact inverse proportion ✓ The
small piece flies off eight times quicker.
**Why the masses go as R³.** Every nucleus has essentially the same density, about
2·3 x 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³ ✓ so mass is proportional to volume, and volume to R³. Doubling the
radius multiplies the mass by **eight**.
**Equivalently, in terms of mass numbers.** R = R₀A^(1/3), so A ∝ R³ ✓ A radius ratio of
1 : 2 means a mass-number ratio of 1 : 8 - for instance, fragments with A = 30 and
A = 240.
**How the kinetic energy divides.** With equal momenta, E = p²/2m, so
E₁/E₂ = m₂/m₁ = **8 : 1** ✓
The **light** fragment carries eight times the energy - which is why in real fission the
lighter fragment is the more penetrating.
**A worked instance.** Take m₁ = 1 unit at 8 m s⁻¹ and m₂ = 8 units at 1 m s⁻¹:
momentum: 8 and 8 ✓ equal and opposite
energy: ½(1)(64) = **32** and ½(8)(1) = **4** ✓ in the ratio 8 : 1.
**Why momentum, not energy, is the starting point.** The parent was at rest, so the
total momentum is **zero** and must remain so ✓ The total kinetic energy, by contrast,
**increases** - it comes from the nuclear binding energy released.
**Reading the distractors.** **2 : 1** ✗ uses the radius ratio directly, forgetting the
cube. **4 : 1** ✗ uses the square, as if mass went with area. **6 : 1** ✗ matches no
power ✓
∴ 8 : 1.

Convert each percentage **decayed** into a number of half-lives, then subtract the
times.
**Step 1 — handle 50% decay.** Half the sample is gone, so half remains:
**one** half-life = **20 minutes** ✓
**Step 2 — handle 87·5% decay.** The fraction **remaining** is
100 − 87·5 = **12·5% = 1/8** ✓
and 1/8 = (½)³, so **three** half-lives = 3 x 20 = **60 minutes** ✓
**Step 3 — subtract.**
60 − 20 = **40 minutes** ✓
**Why work with the fraction remaining.** The decay law is written for what is **left**,
N = N₀(½)^(t/T) ✓ Converting "87·5% decayed" into "12·5% remaining" is the step that
turns the problem into a clean power of two.
**The sequence of half-lives.**
0 min: **100%** remaining, 0% decayed
20 min: **50%** remaining, 50% decayed ✓
40 min: **25%** remaining, 75% decayed
60 min: **12·5%** remaining, 87·5% decayed ✓
**Why the interval is two half-lives.** Going from 50% remaining to 12·5% remaining is a
fall by a factor of **four**, that is two further halvings ✓ so the interval is
2 x 20 = 40 minutes.
**Why 87·5% is chosen.** Because 12·5% is exactly 1/8, a clean power of two ✓ An
awkward figure like 60% decayed would need logarithms:
t = T log(1/0·4)/log 2 = **26·4 min**.
**The general formula, for reference.**
t = T log₂(N₀/N) ✓
Here log₂(8) = 3 and log₂(2) = 1, giving 60 and 20 minutes.
**A caution.** The question asks for the **interval between** the two instants, not the
time to reach the second ✓ Answering 60 minutes would be answering a different
question - and 60 is deliberately not among the options.
**Reading the distractors.** **30 minutes** ✗ and **25 minutes** ✗ correspond to no
whole number of half-lives. **10 minutes** ✗ is half a half-life ✓ The interval must be
a multiple of 20 min, which only 40 is.
∴ 40 minutes.

An **isotope** has the same Z, so the emissions must leave the atomic number unchanged.
**Step 1 — recall the changes.**
**alpha**: Z **−2**, A **−4** ✓
**beta**: Z **+1**, A unchanged ✓
**Step 2 — impose the isotope condition.** For the product to be an isotope of the
original, the net change in **Z** must be **zero** while A changes ✓
**Step 3 — test one alpha and two betas.**
Z: −2 + 1 + 1 = **0** ✓
A: −4 + 0 + 0 = **−4** ✓
Same element, mass number four less - an **isotope** ✓
**Step 4 — test the alternatives.**
**one α and four β**: Z = −2 + 4 = **+2** ✗ two elements along
**one α and one β**: Z = −2 + 1 = **−1** ✗ one element back
**four α and one β**: Z = −8 + 1 = **−7** ✗
Only the second combination returns Z to its starting value ✓
**A worked instance from nature.**
²³⁸₉₂U → ²³⁴₉₀Th + α
²³⁴₉₀Th → ²³⁴₉₁Pa + β
²³⁴₉₁Pa → ²³⁴₉₂U + β ✓
ending at ²³⁴U, an isotope of the parent ²³⁸U - a real segment of the uranium series.
**Why this α-β-β pattern recurs.** Alpha decay removes two protons and two neutrons,
leaving the daughter **neutron-rich** relative to the line of stability ✓ Two beta
decays then convert two neutrons into protons and restore the balance - which is why
the natural decay chains are full of this motif.
**Why the order does not matter.** The changes in Z and A simply add ✓ β-α-β and β-β-α
give the same final nuclide.
**The general rule.** To return to the same element after **n** alpha emissions, exactly
**2n** beta emissions are needed ✓ Here n = 1, so two betas.
**A check on the neutron count.** The daughter has
N = (A − 4) − Z versus the parent's A − Z, so **four fewer neutrons** ✓ two carried off
in the alpha and two converted into protons.
∴ one α and two β.

Convert the mass defect to energy with **1 u = 931·5 MeV**, then divide by the number of
nucleons.
**Step 1 — find the total binding energy.**
BE = Δm x 931·5
= 0·03 x 931·5
= **27·945 MeV** ✓
**Step 2 — divide by the mass number.** Helium-4 has **4** nucleons:
BE/A = 27·945/4
= **6·99 ≈ 6·9825 MeV** ✓
**Where 931·5 MeV/u comes from.** From E = mc² with 1 u = 1·66 x 10⁻²⁷ kg:
E = (1·66 x 10⁻²⁷)(3 x 10⁸)²/(1·6 x 10⁻¹³ J per MeV) = **931·5 MeV** ✓
It is the single most useful conversion factor in nuclear physics.
**What the mass defect is.** The helium nucleus weighs **less** than its four separate
nucleons ✓
2 protons + 2 neutrons: 2(1·00728) + 2(1·00866) = **4·03188 u**
helium nucleus: **4·00150 u**
difference: **0·0304 u** ✓ matching the 0·03 u given, and that missing mass is the
binding energy.
**Why helium-4 is exceptionally stable.** Its real binding energy per nucleon is
**7·07 MeV**, far above its neighbours lithium and beryllium ✓ Two protons and two
neutrons fill the lowest shell completely - a **doubly magic** nucleus. That stability
is why alpha particles are emitted as units in alpha decay, and why helium is the end
product of hydrogen fusion in stars.
**Where it sits on the curve.** The binding-energy curve peaks near **8·8 MeV** at
iron-56 ✓ Helium's 7 MeV is already remarkably high for so light a nucleus - it stands
out as a spike on the rising part of the curve.
**Why binding energy per nucleon is the useful measure.** It allows nuclei of different
sizes to be compared ✓ The **total** binding energy of uranium is far greater than
helium's, but per nucleon uranium is the less tightly bound - which is why it can
fission and release energy.
**Reading the distractors.** **27·93 MeV** ✗ is the **total** binding energy, not the
figure per nucleon - the commonest slip. **2·793** ✗ and **69·825** ✗ are that value
shifted by factors of ten ✓
∴ 6.9825.

For the resultant to have the **same amplitude** as each wave, the phase difference must
be **120°**.
**Step 1 — write the resultant of two equal waves.** For amplitudes a and a with phase
difference φ,
R = **2a cos(φ/2)** ✓
**Step 2 — impose the condition.** The resultant equals a single wave's amplitude:
2a cos(φ/2) = a
**Step 3 — solve.**
cos(φ/2) = **1/2**
φ/2 = 60°
**φ = 120° = 2π/3** ✓
**A check by the general formula.**
R² = a₁² + a₂² + 2a₁a₂ cos φ
= a² + a² + 2a² cos 120°
= 2a² + 2a²(−½)
= **a²** ✓ so R = a, as required.
**Why the phase must be obtuse.** cos 120° is **negative**, so the two waves partly
cancel ✓ A smaller phase difference would give a resultant **larger** than a, and a
larger one would give something smaller.
**The full range of resultants.**
φ = 0: R = **2a** - complete constructive interference ✓
φ = 2π/3: R = **a** ✓ our case
φ = π/2: R = **a√2**
φ = π: R = **0** - complete destructive interference ✓
**The vector picture.** Two equal phasors at 120° form two sides of an **equilateral
triangle**, and the third side - the resultant - is equal to each of them ✓ That is why
the answer is 120° and not some awkward angle: the geometry is as symmetric as it can
be.
**Where three waves at 120° appear.** Three equal phasors at 120° to one another sum to
**exactly zero** ✓ which is the principle of **three-phase** electrical supply: the
three line currents cancel in the neutral.
**Why the intensity is the same too.** Intensity goes as amplitude squared, so equal
amplitudes mean equal intensities ✓ The combined wave carries the same intensity as one
of its constituents - the other wave's energy having been redistributed, not destroyed.
**Reading the distractors.** **π/3 = 60°** ✗ gives R = 2a cos 30° = **1·73a**. **π** ✗
gives **zero**, and **zero** ✗ gives **2a** ✓ Only 2π/3 returns the original amplitude.
∴ 2π/3.
